## SIP TRUNKING PROVIDERS (NIGERIA) — Agent Research Results

**ConnectSIP (Confirmed Nigeria Provider):**
- Call Rates (all NGN/min): ConnectSIP-to-ConnectSIP FREE, Local/National/Mobile (all carriers) = NGN 10.2/min (Airtel, Etisalat, Glo, MTN, Nitel, Visafone)
- Features: IVR, call routing, call recording, 99.99% uptime, instant provisioning, real Nigerian numbers, optimized routing
- Works with 3CX, FreePBX, VICIdial, or ConnectSIP hosted PBX
- URLs: connectsip.com, connectsip.com/support/call-rates

1. Global Call Forwarding — starting $25 + local number cost

5. Netcat Solutions (netcatsolutions.ng) — local/national/toll-free/virtual, "cheaper rates" positioning
6. Others: Cloudonix, Telnyx (global SIP backbone)

**Africa's Talking (Legacy Comparison):**
- Voice API: IVR, call recording/routing, dynamic queuing, webhook callbacks via `callNotificationUrl`, call center support, 2FA
- Toll-free numbers available (user not charged, AT billed)

- IVR, Contact Center, Conferencing, Alerts, Call routing/forwarding, Virtual numbers
- Voice call rates in Nigeria = "Coming Soon"
- Local currency (NGN) pay-as-you-go
- Channels: SMS, WhatsApp, Email, Voice, USSD, SIP trunking

## ELEVENLABS IMPACT PROGRAM (lines ~4014-4072)

Naomi received email from Richard Cave (ElevenLabs Partnerships):
- **Offer:** Complimentary Creator plan for one year, 100,000 credits/month
- **Activation deadline:** April 3, 2026

- **Requirements:** Add ElevenLabs logo to website (with hyperlink), social media post with #ElevenLabs @elevenlabsio, send high-res square logo

**Math on 100K credits:**
- ~750 characters per minute of speech
- 100K credits = ~133 minutes of TTS total
- One Sabi call uses ~2,400 characters (8 responses x 300 chars)
- 100K credits = ~41 calls/month
- 30 kids (480 calls/month) would burn through in ~2 days
- 150 kids (2,400 calls/month) = 1.85% coverage

**Decision:** Chatterbox (free, unlimited, Naomi's voice) for phone pilot. ElevenLabs 100K credits for web demo only (low volume, high quality for demos/investors).

- Total gap: ~$507B/year (education + health + employment)
- Education estimated at 40-50% of total = ~$200-250B/year

**World Bank HOPE-EDU:**

## Lines 9770-10040: CSEA/IDRC Discovery — The Real $40B Source

Naomi shared a PDF from Associates for Change: `https://www.associatesforchange.org/new-reports-2022/Economic%20Costs%20of%20OOSC%20by%20Nigeria.pdf`

**The actual source chain for $40B:**
- Published by: CSEA (Centre for the Study of the Economies of Africa) + IDRC (International Development Research Centre, Canada)
- **NOT SBM Intelligence** — SBM/TheCable just reported on it
- Methodology from Milan &amp; Burnett (2014): "Exclusion from Education: The Economic Cost of Out of School Children in 20 Countries" — Results for Development

**Two approaches:**
- **Micro approach: 7.83% of GDP = ~$40B** (individual wage premiums)
- **Macro approach: 13.03% of GDP = ~$56B** (Barro &amp; Lee growth regression with externalities)

The report states: "If we take the conservative estimate from micro approach, OOSC costs the economy about 7.83% of the GDP per annum. This amounts to about USD 40billion (current US$)."

At 2013 values: GDP ~$510B, OOSC = 10.5M. Current: GDP $285B but OOSC rose to 18.3M (74% increase). The percentage applied to current conditions gives ~$39B — still roughly $40B.

## Lines 10040-10210: Detailed $40B Methodology Explanation

**Micro approach step-by-step:**
1. OOSC count: 10.5 million (MICS 2013)
2. Wage premium from primary: ~15% total for 6 years (2.5%/year, Aromolaran 2004)
3. Secondary cascade: (probability of secondary IF finish primary) × (secondary wage premium) = additional weighted loss
4. Sum across all 10.5M children
5. Express as % of GDP: 7.83% per annum

**Macro approach:** Barro &amp; Lee (2010) growth regression — effect of additional year of schooling on GDP per capita, controls for capital stock and parental income. Captures externalities: innovation, governance, healthcare, foreign investment.

**What it does NOT include:** 23M children who ARE in school but can't read, adults who were OOSC, intergenerational compounding.

**"Per year" means:** The annual GDP shortfall from uneducated workers — recurring, not one-time. New OOSC cohort every year compounds the drag.

## Lines 10210-10600: Tracing Every Number in the Calculation

**All sources traced to original papers:**

1. **OOSC Count 10.5M:** UNICEF, MICS 2013, current = 18.3M (UNICEF 2024, 74% increase)
2. **Wage premium — Aromolaran (2004):** "Wage Returns to Schooling in Nigeria," African Development Review 16(3), 433-455. Returns: 2-3% per year primary, ~4% secondary, 10-15% post-secondary. Uses Mincerian earnings function on Nigerian GHS data.
3. **Global returns — Psacharopoulos &amp; Patrinos (2004):** Education Economics 12(2), 111-134. Global average ~10%/year across 98 countries.
4. **Macro model — Barro &amp; Lee (2010):** NBER Working Paper 15902. Return to additional year: 5-12% after controls. 146 countries, 1950-2010.
5. **Milan &amp; Burnett (2014):** R4D, commissioned by Educate A Child/Education Above All Foundation. Applied across 20 countries. Typical country forfeits 1-2% of GDP from OOSC (micro).
6. **The 7.83% and 13.03%:** CSEA/IDRC Nigeria-specific application of Milan &amp; Burnett methodology.

**GDP discrepancy resolved:** Table 1 showed "$66B" for Nigeria but text says $40B at 7.83%. Nigeria's 2013 GDP was $509-515B (World Bank, current US$). 7.83% × $510B = ~$40B. The Table 1 column must show something else (possibly macro cost estimate for cross-country comparison).

**Naomi's question: Did they actually use Aromolaran?**
Claude admitted assumption was wrong. The CSEA report cites Psacharopoulos &amp; Patrinos (2004) and Colclough et al. (2009), NOT Aromolaran. References list: Milan &amp; Burnett (2014, 2015), Psacharopoulos &amp; Patrinos (2004), Patrinos et al. (2014), Barro &amp; Lee (2010).

**The actual wage premiums from Milan &amp; Burnett paper (found in Naomi's Downloads):**

From Tables 1-4 of the original paper:

| Input | Nigeria Value | Source |
|-------|-------------|--------|
| % Non-Completing OOSC | 23.7% | Table 1 (UIS/MICS) |
| Wage Premium to Primary | 30.0% | Table 2 (Psacharopoulos &amp; Patrinos 2011, Colclough et al. 2009) |
| GDP Loss from Foregone Primary | 7.12% | 23.7% × 30.0% |

Secondary cascade (Table 3):
| Rate of Continuation to Secondary | 43% | GMR 2012 (proxy, data unavailable for Nigeria) |
| Wage Premium to Secondary | 14.0% | Psacharopoulos &amp; Patrinos 2011 |
| Secondary Completion Rate | 50% | Conservative assumption |
| Probability-Weighted Secondary Loss | 0.71% of GDP |

**Total: 7.12% + 0.71% = 7.83% of GDP = ~$40B**

Nigeria's 30% primary wage premium is one of the highest in the sample (Cote d'Ivoire gets 25.7%, Ghana gets 8.9%).

## Lines 10600-10720: Own Calculations Using Aromolaran Data

**Using Nigeria-specific wage returns (Aromolaran 2004):**

With 2013 OOSC rate (23.7%):
- Primary: 23.7% × 15% = 3.56% of GDP
- Secondary: 23.7% × 20% × 60% × 50% = 1.42%
- Total: 4.98% of GDP = ~$14.2B at $285B GDP

With current OOSC rate (~41.3%, scaled from 18.3M/10.5M):
- Primary: 41.3% × 15% = 6.20%
- Secondary: 41.3% × 20% × 60% × 50% = 2.48%
- Total: 8.68% of GDP = ~$24.7B

**Comparison table:**
| Scenario | GDP Loss | Dollar Value |
|----------|---------|-------------|
| Aromolaran wages + 2013 OOSC | 4.98% | ~$14B |
| Aromolaran wages + current OOSC | 8.68% | ~$25B |
| Milan &amp; Burnett global wages + 2013 | 7.83% | ~$40B |

The $40B uses global wage premiums 2x Nigeria's actual measured returns.

**Lines 12310-12520: Research checklist with answers**

**1. Focus group sizing:** 5-10 children is the sweet spot (Nielsen Norman Group: 5 users find 85% of usability issues). 2 weeks ideal. Key metric: voluntary return rate — if 8/10 kids call back on day 2 without being told to, the product works.

**2. Which LGA to start in:** LASUBEB identified 10 high-burden LGAs. Top candidates from data:
- Ajeromi-Ifelodun — highest population density, severe undersupply of public schools, World Bank flagged it
- Alimosho — largest LGA by population (~2M), most schools but most overcrowded
- Mushin — high poverty, high density, major market area (hawking children)
- Oshodi-Isolo — Project Zero specifically enrolled children here
- Agege, Ifako-Ijaiye, Kosofe — likely top 10 by density and poverty
- Recommendation: Start in Mushin or Ajeromi-Ifelodun. Ask Dr. Sonia Ivie for actual LASUBEB data.

**3. Training Ollama to match Claude via RAG:** Already have RAG infrastructure (lib/rag/chunk.ts, lib/rag/retrieval.ts, 916 embeddings seeded in Supabase). During focus group log every Claude Haiku response for QLoRA fine-tuning on Hetzner RTX 4000 (20GB VRAM, proven feasible). RAG reduces quality gap — Llama doesn't need to "know" curriculum, just teach well with right context.

**4. Embedded marketing as revenue model:** Yes, well-established. Viamo's 3-2-1 service does exactly this in 20+ countries. Sabi's lessons naturally use market scenarios ("You bought 50 naira of MTN recharge card...") — pedagogically sound embedded marketing. Airtel contributed $3.2M in free airtime across 15+ countries through Viamo. MTN Foundation spends millions on CSR annually.

**5. Building in public for recruitment:** Post pilot updates, share anonymized data, document journey. Build in public for awareness/grants/hiring, not for pilot recruitment (use board connections for that).

**6. Hiring needs:** Immediate (pilot): don't need to hire. Post-pilot: Lagos-based field coordinator for school relationships and logistics. Long-term: one backend engineer + content developer.

**7. Adult learning market TAM/SAM:** From Technovation app: TAM ~97M (51.6M children + ~45M illiterate adults), SAM ~90M (phone access). Voice-deliverable courses: job interview prep, financial literacy, English proficiency, trade skills (tailoring measurements, carpentry calculations, agricultural practices), exam prep (WAEC/NECO), health literacy. At 1% of 90M at 500 naira/month: $281,000/month = $3.4M/year. At 1,000 naira/month: $6.8M/year.

**8. Private school tutoring market:** Nigerian private schools spend 20,000-50,000 naira/month on IGCSE/Cambridge tutors, 50,000-100,000 naira/month on SAT/AP prep. Sabi at 5,000-10,000 naira/month. 100 schools x 50 students x 5,000 naira/month = 25M naira/month = $187,000/year.

**9. Full subject content via voice:** Already designed in SABI_VOICE_LESSON_DESIGN.md. 1 app lesson (12 min) = 2-3 voice calls (5-7 min each). 286 Cambridge Grade 4 lessons = ~700 voice calls. Content mapping ratios: Math 1:2.5, English 1:2, Science 1:2, Social Studies 1:1.5. Science/Social Studies need visual aids — solution: SMS delivers images alongside voice (dual-channel), or printed materials (200-500 naira per set).

**10. Lagos $25M Education Fund (LEAF):** Announced March 14, 2026. $25M in outcomes-based financing to enroll 50,000+ OOSC ages 6-14. Exactly Sabi's target. Outcomes-based = they pay for results, aligns with Sabi's measurable TaRL assessments.

- LLM (with system prompt + memory + RAG): ~2-4s
- Chatterbox TTS (200-400 char): ~2-4s
- Realistic total: ~5-9 seconds per turn, call it ~7 seconds

### Lines 6062-6380: Agent result -- All sabi-server Python code (16 files, complete technical summary)

**(Full technical details of all 16 files -- main.py, voice.py, voice_twilio.py, voice_asterisk.py, llm.py, memory.py, stt.py, tts.py, answer_matcher.py, secret_loader.py, chatterbox-tts/server.py, docker-compose.yml, requirements.txt, nginx.conf, extensions.conf, pjsip.conf)**

Key highlights not covered elsewhere:

**main.py:** `detect_exaggeration(text)` maps LLM response emotions to Chatterbox exaggeration levels (celebratory=0.75, empathetic=0.35, encouraging=0.6, default=0.5). `ami_originate(phone)` opens TCP socket to Asterisk AMI, waits 2 seconds so child's phone stops ringing, then originates callback.

**voice.py:** Conversation loop driven by AT's webhook model -- each `&lt;Record&gt;` callback creates recursive turn-by-turn loop. Wrap-up after 10+ user turns or detecting phrases like "call me back", "bye", "well done today".

**voice_twilio.py:** Uses **static greeting** ("Hello! My name is Sahbee...") instead of LLM-generated -- deliberate latency optimization. Confidence threshold 0.4 (vs 0.5 for AT).

**voice_asterisk.py:** FastAGI handler. Unlike webhook-driven AT/Twilio, uses persistent TCP connection. Audio must be converted to 8kHz mono WAV for Asterisk telephony codecs.

**llm.py:** `SABI_CORE_PROMPT` -- ~70 lines defining personality, naira-first/abstract-second pedagogy, 1-3 sentence responses, [laugh]/[chuckle]/[sigh] paralinguistic tags, Lagos market scenarios, 5-7 minute lesson structure. Uses `claude-haiku-4-5-20251001`, max_tokens=200. Ollama fallback with temperature=0.7, top_p=0.9, repeat_penalty=1.2.

**memory.py:** For new students (module 0, no sessions): returns "run diagnostic" prompt. For returning students: queries last 5 sessions, builds context with name, session count, module/level, accuracy stats, per-skill breakdown.

**stt.py:** `NIGERIAN_ENGLISH_PROMPT` biases Whisper decoder toward Nigerian vocabulary (naira, kobo, garri, suya, okada, danfo, keke, oya, wahala, sharp sharp). Uses large-v3 model, beam_size=5, VAD filtering.

**answer_matcher.py:** `WORD_TO_NUM` includes Nigerian phonetic variants: "wan"-&gt;1, "tu"-&gt;2, "tree"-&gt;3, "fo"-&gt;4, "fife"-&gt;5, "sik"-&gt;6, "tin"-&gt;10, "twenti"-&gt;20, "tirty"-&gt;30, "foty"-&gt;40, "undred"-&gt;100. Multi-strategy matching: exact (1.0), numeric (0.95), substring (0.8), reverse containment (0.7), Levenshtein.

**chatterbox-tts/server.py:** Chatterbox Turbo (350M params, MIT license). Maps "Sabi" to "Sahbee" pronunciation. Exaggeration parameter 0.25-2.0 controls emotion. Runs on port 8001 as separate container.

**docker-compose.yml:** 6 containers: asterisk (SIP), ollama (LLM), sabi (main server), chatterbox-tts, nginx (proxy), certbot (SSL). Stack requires 3 NVIDIA GPUs or time-sharing 1 GPU.

**extensions.conf:** Flash callback: incoming call from AT is immediately hung up WITHOUT answering (no billing). Hangup event fires curl POST to trigger AMI Originate callback.

**pjsip.conf:** AT uses IP-based authentication (whitelist 136.243.8.51). AT SIP server address still placeholder.

### Lines 6383-6667: Agent result -- All curriculum-app code (30 files, complete technical summary)

**Architecture:** Next.js App Router serving two channels: Curriculum Web App (Clerk auth, Supabase) + Sabi Voice AI Tutor.

**Pages:** page.tsx (landing), layout.tsx (root), sabi-demo/page.tsx (text+voice demo), sabi-voice/page.tsx (phone call simulation), sabi/page.tsx (Sabi landing), dashboard/page.tsx (student progress), subjects/page.tsx (course listing), about/page.tsx.

**API Routes:**
- POST /api/sabi -- text chat endpoint, calls callSabi() with 300 max tokens
- POST /api/sabi/voice/incoming -- Twilio webhook, creates call state in Supabase, generates greeting, returns TwiML Gather with en-GH speech recognition
- POST /api/sabi/voice/respond -- processes speech, manages conversation, auto-wraps at 12 turns, 11 regex wrap-up patterns
- POST /api/sabi/voice/llm -- OpenAI-compatible endpoint for ElevenLabs Custom LLM, streams via anthropic.messages.stream()
- POST /api/sabi/voice-chat -- full pipeline: Groq Whisper STT -&gt; Claude Haiku -&gt; TTS (3-tier fallback)
- POST /api/sabi/tts -- text-to-speech conversion
- POST /api/sabi/stt -- speech-to-text via Groq Whisper

**Libraries:**
- sabi-shared.ts: Core Sabi logic, SABI_CORE_PROMPT (~5,000 tokens), MODULE_CURRICULUM (7 modules), RAG integration
- tts-client.ts: 3-tier fallback (YarnGPT -&gt; Chatterbox -&gt; ElevenLabs), emotion detection for Chatterbox exaggeration
- twiml.ts: TwiML builders, en-GH language, Polly.Amy voice
- call-state.ts: Supabase `sabi_active_calls` table for stateless Vercel
- yarngpt-client.ts: YarnGPT API, Wura default voice, 2000 char limit
- sms.ts: AT preferred for Nigeria, Twilio fallback. Session summaries, practice questions with answer checking, daily reminders
- at-xml.ts: Africa's Talking voice XML builders

**RAG:**
- chunk.ts: Splits curriculum into semantic chunks (concept, example, practice, story, summary)
- retrieval.ts: Supabase pgvector search, 2 module-specific + 2 general chunks

**Curriculum Data:**
- curriculum.ts: Type definitions, subjects array (Foundational Literacy, Numeracy, Math, English, Science, Social Studies)
- foundational-literacy.ts: ~69,000 tokens, Nigerian cultural context
- foundational-numeracy.ts: ~87,000 tokens, Nigerian market scenarios

**Middleware:** Demo access control (key-based), subdomain routing (sabi.*), Clerk auth for /dashboard

On slide:

Child dials → Sabi answers, asks their name
         → Runs diagnostic through conversation
         → Teaches at THEIR level, not grade level
         → 5-7 min call, one concept, Nigerian market scenarios
         → Child hangs up, calls back tomorrow
         → Sabi remembers everything

"You buy pure water for 20 naira and groundnuts for 30 naira.
 How much altogether?"

Children solve market math 9x better than abstract math.
— Nature 2025, Sokoto Nigeria study
Speaker notes:
"Here's what happens. A child calls. Sabi asks their name, runs a quick diagnostic through conversation — not a test, a game. 'You buy pure water for twenty naira and groundnuts for thirty — how much altogether?' Based on their answers, Sabi places them at their actual learning level. A fifth-grader reading at a second-grade level gets second-grade content.

Every call is five to seven minutes. One concept. All in Nigerian market scenarios — because a Nature study found children solve math nine times more often when it's framed as a real market transaction. If they get three right, difficulty increases. If they struggle, Sabi scaffolds — never says 'wrong,' just rephrases with smaller numbers.

And when they call back tomorrow, Sabi remembers their name, their level, their mistakes. Multiple kids sharing one family phone each get their own profile."

Background: Off-white/cream (#FAFAF5) — NOT pure white (too sterile)
Primary text: Near-black (#1A1A1A)

Secondary accent: Teal (#075449) — only for data/numbers/tech slides
Fonts: DM Sans (headings, bold) + Inter (body, clean)

## WHAT THE DOC SAYS VS REALITY (load test corrected)

The doc was written March 9 before the load test on March 31. The load test showed Whisper + Chatterbox + Ollama fighting over the same GPU causes massive slowdowns at 5+ concurrent calls (TTS went from 1.5s to 14s). So the "1 GPU = 5,000-10,000 students" claim is wrong.

**Real capacity per GPU: ~300-500 students** (not 5,000-10,000)

| What the doc says | Reality (load-tested) | Why |
|---|---|---|
| 1 GPU = 5,000-10,000 students | 1 GPU = 300-500 students | GPU contention — 3 models sharing 20GB VRAM |
| $0.41/student at 5,000 + zero-rating | $5-8/student at 5,000 + zero-rating | Need 10-15 servers, not 1 |
| $0.10/student at 100,000 | $1-2/student at 100,000 | Need ~250 servers |

The $8K is almost entirely operational — you're not building anything, you're running what's already built with real children.

**Things that cost basically nothing:**
- STT (Whisper, self-hosted): $0
- TTS (Chatterbox, self-hosted): $0

- **Claude Haiku: $0.0045/call** — temporary. Eliminated when Ollama quality is sufficient

## Naomi · 2026-04-16T00:03:34.510Z

How much do we need for telephony toll free for our pilot

## Claude · 2026-04-16T00:04:02.436Z

Based on everything I've read, here's the honest answer:

## You don't need toll-free for the pilot.

The whole point of the flash callback model is that it's **functionally free for the child** without paying toll-free rates. Here's how it works:

**Flash callback flow:**
1. Child dials Sabi's AT number
2. Call rings once, Sabi hangs up BEFORE answering (child pays ₦0)
3. Sabi calls the child back via AT SIP outbound at ₦3/min
4. **Child pays nothing. You pay ₦3/min ($0.00188/min)**

That's what you're already set up to do with Africa's Talking.

---

## Toll-free vs Flash Callback — the math for 300 kids, 6 months

| Model | Per-minute rate | Total cost (504,000 min) | Per student |
|---|---|---|---|
| **AT flash callback** | ₦3/min ($0.00188) | **$948** | **$3.16** |
| **Alpha toll-free** | ₦14/min ($0.00875) | **$4,410** | **$14.70** |
| **InfoTek toll-free** | ₦18/min ($0.01125) | **$5,670** | **$18.90** |

Toll-free is **4.7x to 6x more expensive** and gives you the exact same result — the child pays nothing either way.

The only advantage of toll-free is the child doesn't need to know to "beep and wait." They just dial and stay on. But for a pilot where you're recruiting through schools and your advisory board, you can explain the beep-and-callback in 10 seconds.

---

## If you still want toll-free pricing

From the research and the InfoTek invoice you received:

**Alpha Technologies (AT's toll-free partner):**
- Per-minute: ₦14/min ($0.00875)
- SIP unlimited channels: ₦688,538/year (~$430/year)
- Deposit: ₦200,000 (~$125)
- Activation: 24 hours
- **First year total: ~$555 setup + per-minute usage**

**InfoTek PS:**
- Per-minute: ₦18/min ($0.01125)
- 20 concurrent SIP channels: ₦1,300,000/year (~$813/year)
- Deposit: ₦500,000 (~$313)
- **First year total: ~$1,126 setup + per-minute usage**

**For 300 kids, 6 months on Alpha toll-free:**

| Item | Cost |
|---|---|
| Alpha SIP annual | $430 |
| Alpha deposit (refundable) | $125 |
| Toll-free minutes (504,000 x $0.00875) | $4,410 |
| **Total** | **$4,965** |
| **Per student** | **$16.55** |

vs flash callback: **$948 total, $3.16/student**

You'd burn $4,000 extra for no learning outcome difference.

---

## Bottom line

**For the pilot, budget $948 for telephony** (flash callback on AT). That's what's in your NVA application and it's the right call.

Save toll-free for Phase 3 when you're pitching telcos to zero-rate the line — at that point the telco pays, not you. Or if you win a grant large enough that $4K for toll-free is trivial compared to the convenience.

The $500 telephony line item in your NVA budget covers the focus group + the first ~3 months of the pilot. The full 6-month pilot telephony is $948 — the remaining $448 comes from the $3,325 contingency buffer.

## Lagos Field Coordinator Salary — What You'd Actually Pay

### Market rates for a program/field coordinator at an NGO in Lagos:

| Experience Level | Monthly (NGN) | Monthly (USD) | Annual (NGN) | Annual (USD) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Junior** (< 2 years) | ₦150,000-250,000 | $94-156 | ₦1.8M-3M | $1,125-1,875 |
| **Mid-level** (2-5 years) | ₦250,000-400,000 | $156-250 | ₦3M-4.8M | $1,875-3,000 |
| **Senior** (5-10 years) | ₦400,000-600,000 | $250-375 | ₦4.8M-7.2M | $3,000-4,500 |

The average across sources lands around **₦280,000-350,000/month ($175-220/month)** for a mid-level coordinator in Lagos.

### What "high quality" means for your specific needs:

This person needs to:
- Recruit 300 children from Mushin/Ajeromi-Ifelodun LGAs
- Coordinate with schools and market women
- Make sure kids actually call Sabi daily
- Distribute printed literacy materials (Phase 2)
- Handle parent communication
- Run pre/post TaRL assessments
- Report data back to you at Wesleyan

That's a **mid-level education program coordinator** — someone who already has relationships in Lagos public schools or community organizations. Not entry-level.

### My recommendation: ₦300,000-400,000/month ($188-250/month)

**Why this range:**
- ₦300K is competitive vs the NGO average (~₦262K) — attracts quality candidates who have options
- ₦400K is the upper bound for a coordinator role (above that you're in manager territory)
- For context: median Lagos salary is ₦351K/month across all sectors, so this is right at market
- A government primary school teacher makes ₦50,000-150,000/month — so your coordinator earns 2-3x a teacher, which signals you're serious

## Hetzner Setup Fee

Yes — **EUR 79 (~$87) one-time setup fee**. You already paid this when the server was provisioned on March 10. It's not a recurring cost. But it should be in the total if you're calculating "what did this cost from zero."

---

## Your Wages — What You Can Legally Pay Yourself

### The IRS rule for 501(c)(3):
You **can** pay yourself a salary. The IRS requires it to be "reasonable compensation" — meaning what similar organizations pay for similar roles. The board votes on it, and you recuse yourself from that vote. It must be payment for real work, not a share of profits.

### What's "reasonable" for your situation:

| Benchmark | Hourly | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **Nonprofit ED (small org, national avg)** | $30/hr | [ZipRecruiter](https://www.ziprecruiter.com/Salaries/Non-Profit-Executive-Director-Salary) |
| **Nonprofit ED (Salary.com)** | $55/hr | [Salary.com](https://www.salary.com/research/salary/alternate/executive-director-non-profit-organization-salary) |
| **Small nonprofit ED (budget <$1M)** | $26-41/hr | [CNPC](https://cnpc.coach/nonprofit-executive-director-salary/) ($55K-85K/yr) |
| **Very small nonprofit (budget <$50K)** | $15-25/hr | Derived — proportional to org size |
| **CT minimum wage (2026)** | $16.35/hr | CT DOL |
| **Wesleyan Federal Work-Study** | ~$15-17/hr | Typical campus rate |

### My honest recommendation:

**$20-25/hour** is defensible for your situation. Here's why:

- You're a sole technical founder who built the entire stack — that's not entry-level work. A freelance developer doing what you've done bills $50-150/hr.
- But the org has under $25K in total funding. Paying yourself $50/hr from an $8K grant looks bad to future funders.
- $20-25/hr is above minimum wage, below market rate, and shows you're serious but not extracting value.
- At 10-15 hours/week over 6 months (the pilot): **$5,200-9,750 total**

### The problem:

At $20/hr and 15 hrs/week for 6 months, that's **$7,800** — which eats almost the entire NVA grant. You can't pay yourself AND fund the pilot from $8K.

### What most student founders actually do:

1. **Don't take a salary in Year 1.** Work for free (sweat equity), live off financial aid / campus jobs / family support. This is what Pyari's founders likely did.
2. **Build the stipend into bigger grants.** When you apply for Mastercard ($100K+) or Gates, include "founder stipend: $15,000" as a line item. That's standard and expected.
3. **Use PCE funding for operations, not salary.** The NVA guidelines say funds must be spent on the venture. Paying yourself IS allowed, but judges will notice if 80% of the budget is your salary.
4. **Track your hours anyway.** Even if unpaid now, documenting hours establishes the value of your contribution for future grant budgets and tax purposes.

### If you DO want to include wages in the budget:

| Scenario | Rate | Hours/wk | Duration | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Minimal stipend** | $15/hr | 10 hrs | 6 months | **$3,900** |
| **Moderate** | $20/hr | 10 hrs | 6 months | **$5,200** |
| **Competitive** | $25/hr | 15 hrs | 6 months | **$9,750** |

---

| Category | Item | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| **Already paid** | Hetzner setup fee | $87 (paid March 2026) |

$6,425 without your wages — fits in $8K NVA with $1,575 buffer.

$11,625 with wages — needs NVA ($8K) + one more grant (Technovation $10K, or a portion of it).

My take: don't include wages in the NVA budget. Use the $8K for operations. Include your stipend in the Mastercard / Gates / HOPE-EDU applications where $15-20K for founder compensation is a rounding error on a $100K+ grant.

## Naomi · 2026-04-16T00:28:18.234Z

do we have implications if we're with 501c3 standing? read legal roadmap - are we a non-profit in Nigeria or a non-profit in the U.S.?

## Claude · 2026-04-16T00:28:47.814Z

From the [LEGAL_ROADMAP.md](7. Legal & IP/LEGAL_ROADMAP.md):

You're **both**, phased:

**Phase 1 (now):** US 501(c)(3) nonprofit — "Education for Equality Inc." incorporated in Connecticut. This is the entity that receives grants, owns IP, and is tax-exempt.

**Phase 2 (within 12 months):** Nigerian Incorporated Trustee via CAC — separate Nigerian charitable entity. Receives funds FROM the US entity, implements programs on the ground, has its own board of trustees.

They're **two separate legal entities** in two countries.

---

## The implication you're asking about:

The US 501(c)(3) is sending money to Nigeria to fund a program serving Nigerian children. The IRS has specific rules for this:

**Expenditure responsibility** — when your US nonprofit sends funds to the Nigerian entity (which is NOT a US 501(c)(3)), you must:
- Exercise "expenditure responsibility" over those funds
- Maintain records showing the funds are used for exempt purposes
- Report foreign grants on your Form 990 (or 990-N if under $50K)

**This is standard.** Thousands of US nonprofits fund programs in Africa this way. It's not a problem — it's just paperwork.

**Before the Nigerian CAC registration is done**, you have two options:
1. You (Naomi) travel to Lagos and spend the money directly on program activities — server costs, telephony, materials. The money never goes to a Nigerian entity — it goes to vendors (Hetzner, AT, Alpha). This is simpler and doesn't trigger expenditure responsibility rules.
2. You send money to a Nigerian individual (like a contractor/coordinator) — this is fine as long as it's payment for services, documented with an agreement.

**The Lagos field coordinator** is a Nigerian contractor paid by the US nonprofit. That's a vendor payment, not a foreign grant. Clean and simple — just need a written contractor agreement.

---

## Insurance implications with 501(c)(3) status:

The 501(c)(3) designation itself doesn't require you to carry insurance. But:

- **D&O insurance** protects your board members if someone sues the organization. With a 7-person advisory board including Hon. Folasade Adefisayo and Dr. Sonia Ivie — people with reputations — this becomes more relevant as you grow. Not urgent now at $8K budget, but worth getting before you sign a government contract or take $100K+ in grants.

- **You don't need Nigerian liability insurance** because the US nonprofit isn't registered as an employer in Nigeria, doesn't operate a physical facility in Nigeria, and the children are using their own phones at home.

- **Once you register the Nigerian Incorporated Trustee**, that entity may need its own insurance depending on Nigerian nonprofit regulations. Ask Barrister Adejoke about this when the time comes.

---

## Bottom line for right now:

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Are you a US nonprofit? | **Yes** — CT incorporated, EIN obtained, 501(c)(3) pending |
| Are you a Nigerian nonprofit? | **Not yet** — CAC registration planned within 12 months |
| Can you operate in Nigeria without CAC? | **Yes** — you're a US org paying vendors and contractors in Nigeria. Legal. |
| Do you need insurance? | **Not yet** — no physical operations, no US employees, children at home on phones |
| What do you need to document? | Contractor agreement with Lagos coordinator, receipts for all spending, board minutes approving budget |
| When does this get more complex? | When you (a) register the Nigerian entity, (b) take $100K+ grants, or (c) sign a government contract. Then you need expenditure responsibility reporting, D&O insurance, and possibly a Nigerian audit. |

## Naomi · 2026-04-16T00:30:57.135Z

do I need to travel to Lagos to chekc on the pilot, or is it okay to do it completely remotely?

## Claude · 2026-04-16T00:31:24.399Z

Honestly? You don't **need** to travel. But it depends on what you're optimizing for.

## Can you run it 100% remote?

**Yes.** Here's why:

- The whole point of Sabi is that it works over a phone — you can monitor every call from Connecticut
- Supabase has every student's session data, skill scores, call frequency, module progress
- The Lagos field coordinator handles recruitment, materials distribution, parent communication
- Your advisory board (Dr. Sonia, Rhoda, Remi) are physically in Lagos and can check on things
- You can WhatsApp/call the coordinator daily
- Pre/post TaRL assessments can be administered by the coordinator, not you

**Plenty of nonprofits run international programs remotely.** ConnectEd's researchers at Oxford/Harvard didn't personally sit in every classroom in Botswana.

## Why you might want to go anyway

| Reason | Weight |
|---|---|
| **Credibility with funders** | HIGH — "I was on the ground" hits different in a Mastercard application than "my coordinator reported..." |
| **Credibility with judges** | HIGH — PCE judges will ask "have you been there?" at the April 17 pitch |
| **Troubleshooting** | MEDIUM — hearing a child actually use Sabi on a real phone in a noisy Lagos market tells you things data can't |
| **Relationships** | MEDIUM — meeting school principals face-to-face, sitting with Dr. Sonia at LASUBEB, visiting Mushin |
| **Content** | HIGH — photos and video of real children using Sabi are worth more than any slide deck for future pitches |
| **Motivation** | REAL — you haven't been home in a while. Seeing the kids you're building for changes how you build |

## What changes if you cut the $2,000 travel

Total drops from $6,509 to **$4,509**. That frees up $3,491 in the NVA budget — enough to cover toll-free telephony on Alpha instead of flash callback, or extend the pilot to 9 months, or add a second coordinator.

## My take

**Go to Lagos for 1-2 weeks at the START of the pilot (July), not throughout.** You need to be there for:
1. Meeting the coordinator face-to-face and aligning on process
2. Visiting the schools/communities where children will be recruited
3. Watching the first 5-10 kids use Sabi on real phones — this is your focus group
4. Taking photos and video for every future pitch deck, grant application, and social media post
5. Meeting Dr. Sonia, Rhoda, Remi in person as a board, not just over WhatsApp

Then go home and run it remotely for the remaining 5 months. The coordinator reports weekly, you check Supabase daily, your mom checks in physically when needed.

**$2,000 for a 1-2 week Lagos trip is realistic** — flights from the US are $800-1,200 round trip, and you have family to stay with.

If money is genuinely tight, skip it and run remote. The pilot will still work. But the photos, the stories, and the "I was there" credibility are hard to replace.

This person is going to communities in **Mushin, Ajeromi-Ifelodun, and surrounding LGAs** — these are dense, low-income areas on the mainland. They'll be visiting schools, meeting parents at markets, distributing materials, checking on kids.

- 2-3 community visits/day

## Should transport be separate or included in salary?

Two approaches:

**Option A: Salary includes transport** — Pay ₦400,000/mo ($250) instead of ₦350,000 ($219). Simpler, no receipts needed. But they might pocket the transport money and skip visits.

**Option B: Salary + transport allowance** — ₦350,000 salary + ₦66,000 transport = ₦416,000/mo ($260). Requires basic reporting on where they went. Standard in Nigerian NGOs — most orgs pay transport separately.

Option B is better for accountability. You want to know they actually visited the schools.

## Naomi · 2026-04-16T00:49:09.193Z

how do I find a field coordinator whom I can pay in equity?

## Claude · 2026-04-16T00:49:50.581Z

That's a smart instinct — but there are real constraints with a 501(c)(3).

## The problem: nonprofits don't have equity

A 501(c)(3) has **no owners and no shares**. There's nothing to give. Unlike a startup where you hand out stock options, a nonprofit legally cannot distribute profits or ownership stakes to anyone — that's the core IRS requirement ("no private inurement").

So traditional equity compensation is off the table entirely.

## What you CAN do instead

### 1. Promise a paid role once funded
"I can't pay you market rate now, but when we land the Mastercard grant ($100K+), you become our first full-time Lagos hire at ₦400,000-500,000/month."

This is how most early nonprofits recruit. The person bets on the mission and your ability to raise money. You put it in writing — a letter of intent, not a contract — so they know it's real.

### 2. Title + board seat
Give them **Program Director, Lagos** or **Head of Field Operations** — a title that has career value. If they're good, offer a seat on the Nigerian entity's board of trustees once you register the CAC. Board membership in a growing education nonprofit with World Bank and EKOEXCEL connections is valuable in Lagos.

### 3. Stipend now, salary later
Pay them a reduced stipend (₦150,000-200,000/month instead of ₦350,000) with a written agreement that it increases to ₦400,000+ once grant funding comes in. This cuts your 6-month cost from $1,313 to **$563-750**.

### 4. Revenue share from the future for-profit
Your legal roadmap has a Phase 3: **Nigerian for-profit entity** (EfE Services Ltd or Sabi Education Ltd) for paid adult courses and private school contracts. THAT entity CAN have shareholders. You could offer the coordinator a small equity stake (2-5%) in the future for-profit as part of their compensation package now. Structure it as a written agreement: "When Education for Equality registers a Nigerian Ltd company, you receive X% of shares in exchange for your service during the pilot period."

This is legal. The nonprofit and for-profit are separate entities. The for-profit hasn't been created yet, so you're promising future equity in a company that doesn't exist — essentially a SAFE-style agreement adapted for Nigeria.

### 5. Profit-sharing from adult courses
Similar to above but simpler — instead of equity, promise a percentage of revenue from the paid adult learning channel once it launches. "You get 3% of adult course revenue for 3 years" is easier than equity and doesn't require incorporating the for-profit immediately.

## Where to actually find this person

| Channel | Why it works | How |
|---|---|---|
| **Your mom (Dr. Sonia)** | She manages 1,016 schools and 13,000+ teachers. She knows every ambitious young education worker in Lagos. | Ask her directly: "I need someone in Mushin or Ajeromi who knows the community, is hungry, and will work for a stipend now with a real job later" |
| **Rhoda Odigboh** | CEO of Kizazi, trained 14,000+ educators. Same network. | Same ask |
| **Remi Tanimola** | 20+ years with public primary children. Knows the ground-level people. | Same ask |
| **EKOEXCEL alumni** | Former school support officers or teachers who want to do more than classroom work | Dr. Sonia can identify these |
| **Wesleyan / university networks in Lagos** | UNILAG, LASU, Covenant students or recent grads in education, public health, or social work | Post in alumni WhatsApp groups |
| **Church community** | You mentioned the former Minister of Education is connected through your church. Church networks in Lagos are powerful for finding trustworthy people. | Ask your parents to put the word out |
| **Nelly (TAI for Education)** | She runs a 10,000+ student education program. She may know people. | Ask directly |

## My recommendation

**Go through Dr. Sonia first.** She's the strongest channel because:
- She knows who's good and who's not in Lagos public education
- She can vet for trustworthiness (you're giving this person access to children)
- Someone she recommends will take the role seriously because her reputation backs it
- They'll already understand the school system, LASUBEB, and the communities

**Offer: ₦150,000-200,000/month stipend + Program Director title + written commitment to ₦400,000+ salary when first major grant lands + potential equity in future for-profit entity.**

That drops your 6-month coordinator cost from $1,313 to **$563-750**.

|---|---|---|
| Coordinator (6 months) | $563-750 | $1,313 |
| Transport (6 months) | $500 | $500 |
| **Total staff** | **$1,063-1,250** | **$1,813** |

**Updated grand total with stipend model: ~$5,454-5,641**

## Naomi · 2026-04-16T00:56:27.338Z

why do I need a uspto trademark again?

## Claude · 2026-04-16T00:56:43.559Z

To stop someone in the US from launching an education product called "Sabi" and claiming the name.

But honestly? **You probably don't need it right now.** Here's why:

**The case FOR USPTO ($350-700):**
- Protects "Sabi" in the US market
- Required if you ever want to block a US competitor using the name
- Some US grants/funders like to see IP protection in place

**The case AGAINST (right now):**
- You operate in Nigeria, not the US
- Your users are Nigerian children on feature phones
- Nobody in the US is competing for the name "Sabi" in education
- $350-700 is 3-7% of your entire budget for something that solves zero problems today
- It takes 8-12 months to process anyway — you can file later when you have more money
- The Nigeria NIPO trademark ($150) protects you where you actually operate

**If someone DID launch "Sabi" in the US tomorrow:**
- It wouldn't affect your Nigerian operations at all
- You'd have prior use documentation (website live since Feb 2026, MIT win, copyright brief, git history)
- Prior use gives you common law trademark rights even without registration

**Cut it.** File Nigeria NIPO now ($150), file USPTO in Year 2 when you have $100K+ in grants and US presence actually matters.

Saves **$350-700**.

**Updated total without USPTO:**

| | 1 class cut | Both classes cut |
|---|---|---|
| Savings | $350 | $700 |
| New total | **$13,579** | **$13,229** |

Or on the flash callback stack: **$9,521** (no USPTO) vs $9,871 (with 1 class).

**But** — Lagos traffic is chaos. The per-minute charge adds up fast when you're stuck on Ikorodu Road for 45 minutes. And surge pricing during morning rush (7-10am) and evening (4-8pm) is real. So I'll use the surge numbers for half the trips.

Here's the real picture:

## New Cars in Nigeria

New cars are **extremely expensive** because of import duties (35% + 35% surcharge + VAT):

| Car | New Price (Nigeria) | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Kia Picanto / Rio | ₦15M-22M ($9,375-13,750) | Cheapest new option |
| Hyundai i10 / i20 | ₦18M-25M ($11,250-15,625) | |
| Toyota Corolla | ₦32M+ ($20,000+) | Most popular car in Nigeria |
| Suzuki Alto / Swift | ₦12M-18M ($7,500-11,250) | If available |
| Innoson IVM (Nigerian-made) | ₦8M-15M ($5,000-9,375) | Made in Nigeria, cheaper |

## Used Cars (what people actually buy)

"Tokunbo" (foreign-used, imported) is the Lagos way:

| Car | Used Price | Year Range |
|---|---|---|
| Toyota Corolla | ₦4.5M-10M ($2,800-6,250) | 2008-2015 |
| Toyota Camry | ₦3.7M-12M ($2,300-7,500) | 2008-2016 |
| Honda Civic | ₦3M-8M ($1,875-5,000) | 2006-2014 |
| Kia Rio | ₦3M-7M ($1,875-4,375) | 2012-2018 |
| Hyundai Accent | ₦2.5M-5M ($1,563-3,125) | 2010-2015 |
| **Cheapest reliable tokunbo** | **₦2M-3M ($1,250-1,875)** | Older Corolla/Camry |

## Are you thinking what I think you're thinking?

If you're considering buying a car for the coordinator instead of paying for Bolt/transport allowance:

| Option | 6-month cost | 12-month cost |
|---|---|---|
| Coordinator transport allowance ($500/6mo) | **$500** | **$1,000** |
| Cheapest used car (tokunbo Corolla) | **$2,500-3,500** | Same (one-time) |
| Car + fuel (₦80,000-120,000/mo) | +$300-450 for 6mo | +$600-900 |
| Car + insurance + maintenance | +$200-400 | +$400-800 |
| **Total car ownership (6 months)** | **$3,000-4,350** | **$3,500-5,200** |

A car costs **6-8x more** than the transport allowance for 6 months. Only breaks even after ~3 years. And you'd need to deal with registration, insurance, maintenance, and the car sitting idle if the coordinator leaves.

**Not worth it for a 6-12 month pilot.** Maybe for Year 2 when you have a permanent Lagos office and a $100K+ grant. At that point the car becomes an org asset.

Unless you're thinking about buying a car for yourself while you're there — in which case, same math applies. $106/month in Uber vs $3,000+ for a car you'd use for 1 month.

Sources:

- [Carlots.ng — New Car Prices Nigeria 2025](https://carlots.ng/motoring/new-car-prices-in-nigeria/)
- [Jiji.ng — Toyota Corolla prices](https://jiji.ng/cars/toyota-corolla)
- [Pulse Nigeria — Best Used Cars Under ₦5M](https://www.pulse.ng/articles/lifestyle/5-million-naira-cars-in-nigeria-2025052210264977043)

## Glo costs for 1 month in Lagos

You'll need data for maps/Uber app, WhatsApp with coordinator and board, email, video calls back to the US, general browsing, and some airtime for local calls.

**Data usage estimate:**

| Activity | Daily usage | Monthly |
|---|---|---|
| Uber/Bolt app (maps, booking) | ~200MB | ~6GB |
| WhatsApp (messages, voice notes, photos) | ~150MB | ~4.5GB |
| Email + browsing | ~100MB | ~3GB |
| Video calls (Zoom/FaceTime to US, 2-3x/week) | ~500MB per call x 10 calls | ~5GB |
| Social media / misc | ~200MB | ~6GB |
| **Total** | | **~25GB** |

**Best Glo plan:**

| Plan | Data | Price | Value |
|---|---|---|---|
| ₦8,000 | 25GB | $5 | Tight fit — will run out if you video call a lot |
| **₦10,000** | **32.5GB + 4GB bonus = 36.5GB** | **$6.25** | **Best fit — covers everything with buffer** |
| ₦15,000 | 52.5GB | $9.38 | Overkill unless you're streaming |

**Airtime for calls:**

| What | Estimate |
|---|---|
| Local calls (coordinator, schools, parents) | ~30 min/day x 30 days = 900 min |
| At ₦6.6/min (Glo-to-Glo) or ₦9.3/min (other networks) | ₦5,940-8,370 |
| Round up for access fees + cross-network | **₦10,000 (~$6.25)** |

**Total Glo for 1 month:**

| Item | Cost (₦) | Cost ($) |
|---|---|---|
| Data (₦10,000 plan, 36.5GB) | ₦10,000 | $6.25 |
| Airtime (calls) | ₦10,000 | $6.25 |
| **Total** | **₦20,000** | **$12.50** |

## Claude · 2026-04-16T01:28:37.982Z

Depends on what level you want:

## Use your iPhone (free)

Honestly — your iPhone already shoots 4K video with stabilization. For Lagos pilot photos, kids-using-Sabi videos, social media content, and grant application visuals, your phone is fine. Most nonprofit content is shot on phones. Pyari's deck photos look like they were shot on phones.

## If you want a dedicated camera

| Camera | Price | Best for | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Your iPhone** | **$0** | Everything right now | 4K, good in low light, always with you |
| **GoPro Hero 12** | **$250-350** | Action shots, wide angle, waterproof | Great for field visits, small, durable |
| **Sony ZV-1** | **$350-450** | Video-first, vlogging, interviews | Best compact video camera, no extra lenses needed |
| **Canon EOS R100** | **$400-480** | Photo + video, interchangeable lenses | Cheapest mirrorless, but lenses add cost |
| **DJI Osmo Pocket 3** | **$400-520** | Stabilized handheld video | Gimbal built in, silky smooth footage |
| **Sony ZV-E10 II** | **$700-800** | Serious content, interchangeable lenses | Overkill for pilot but future-proof |

## My take

**Don't buy a camera for the pilot.** Use your phone. Spend the $300-500 on something that actually moves the needle — like extending the coordinator's contract or covering more telephony minutes.

Buy a camera when you have content budget from a $100K+ grant and need professional-quality video for a fundraising campaign or Mastercard application.

If you absolutely want something and have the budget, the **Sony ZV-1 at ~$400** is the sweet spot — compact, great video, no extra lenses, built for exactly this kind of on-the-ground content creation.

Sources:
- [KEH — Budget Cameras for Content Creators 2026](https://www.keh.com/expert-advice/camera-gear/budget-cameras-every-content-creator-needs-in-2026/)
- [OBSBOT — Best Cameras for Social Media Content 2026](https://www.obsbot.com/blog/camera/camera-for-social-media-content)

Good question. Your go-to-market for the pilot is recruiting 300 kids — they need to know the number exists and call it. Here's every channel and what it costs:

## Go-To-Market Channels for the Pilot

### FREE (₦0) — Your primary channels

| Channel | How | Cost | Why it works |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Advisory board word-of-mouth** | Dr. Sonia tells EKOEXCEL teachers, Rhoda tells her network, Remi tells parents she works with | $0 | This is how you recruit 80%+ of your pilot kids. Board members already have relationships with thousands of parents in exactly the LGAs you're targeting. |
| **School announcements** | Coordinator visits partner schools, speaks at morning assembly or PTA meeting | $0 | School head gives you 5 minutes to explain to parents. Most effective recruitment channel for education programs in Lagos. |
| **Church announcements** | Pastor mentions the number at Sunday service | $0 | Your family's church, plus churches in Mushin/Ajeromi. Pastors love promoting free education. One announcement reaches hundreds of families. |
| **WhatsApp groups** | Share a one-paragraph message + the phone number in parents' WhatsApp groups | $0 | Every Lagos school has parent WhatsApp groups. One share = 50-200 parents see it instantly. The coordinator or a teacher shares it. |
| **Word-of-mouth** | First 10 kids tell friends, parents tell other parents at market | $0 | "A phone number spreads itself" — from your pitch deck. |

These free channels alone can recruit 300 kids if your board is active. ConnectEd, Rori AI, and EKOEXCEL all recruited through schools — not advertising.

### LOW COST — Amplifiers

| Channel | What | Unit Cost | Quantity | Total |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Flyers / handbills** | A5 flyer: "FREE AI tutor for your child. Call this number." In English + Pidgin | ₦85-175 each (100 copies = ₦8,500-17,500) | 500 copies | **₦42,500-87,500 ($27-55)** |
| **Banners** | 5ft x 3ft flex banner at school gates or market entrance | ₦6,300-10,000 each | 5 banners (1 per school) | **₦31,500-50,000 ($20-31)** |
| **Posters** | A3 poster for church notice boards, community centers | ₦500-1,000 each | 20 posters | **₦10,000-20,000 ($6-13)** |
| **Market crier / community announcer** | Someone with a megaphone walks through Mushin market announcing | ₦2,000-5,000 per session | 3 sessions | **₦6,000-15,000 ($4-9)** |
| **Graphic design** | Flyer + banner + poster design (one designer, all pieces) | ₦10,000-25,000 | 1 | **₦10,000-25,000 ($6-16)** |

Or — Hakeemah (Neon Nexus, your branding advisor) might do the design free.

### MEDIUM COST — If you want broader reach

| Channel | What | Cost | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Community radio spot** | 30-60 second ad on Lagos community radio (e.g. Radio Lagos, EKO FM) | ₦11,200-18,555 per spot | Even 5 spots = ₦56,000-93,000 ($35-58). Reaches thousands but untargeted — most listeners don't have kids aged 8-14. |
| **Instagram / social media ads** | Targeted ads to Lagos parents | ₦10,000-50,000 ($6-31) | Low priority — your target parents are feature-phone users, not Instagram users. Save for adult learning channel later. |

### NOT NEEDED for pilot

| Channel | Why skip |
|---|---|
| Digital marketing agency | Overkill — ₦200K+/month for 300 kids you can recruit through 3 schools |
| Newspaper ads | Too expensive, wrong audience |
| TV advertising | Way too expensive |
| Billboard | ₦500K+/month, absurd for a 300-kid pilot |
| SMS blast | Need VAS aggregator license at scale, unnecessary for pilot |

## Realistic Go-To-Market Budget

| Tier | What's included | Total |
|---|---|---|
| **₦0 (free channels only)** | Board word-of-mouth + school assemblies + church + WhatsApp groups | **$0** |
| **Basic ($50-75)** | Above + 500 flyers + 5 banners | **$50-75** |
| **Standard ($100-150)** | Above + 20 posters + graphic design + 3 market announcements | **$100-150** |
| **With radio ($150-200)** | Above + 5 community radio spots | **$150-200** |

## My take

**$100-150 is the right budget.** Flyers and banners at school gates do the heavy lifting. WhatsApp + board network does the rest. You don't need radio or social media ads to recruit 300 kids from 5-6 schools where your advisory board already has relationships.

The real "cost" of go-to-market is the **coordinator's time** — which is already budgeted. They're the ones visiting schools, talking to parents at markets, handing out flyers. The materials just support them.

## Where this fits in the $8K NVA budget

That "Content & documentation" line item I put at $380.50 — split it:

| Item | Amount |

| Go-to-market materials (flyers, banners, posters, design) | $150 |
| TaRL assessment printing + parent consent forms | $80 |
| Pilot report design + data visualization | $100 |
| Social media content production | $50 |
| **Total** | **$380** |

## Claude · 2026-04-16T02:10:33.327Z

Okay — to answer both your questions:

## Alpha Technologies: NO USSD

Alpha does **voice only** — toll-free (0800), non-toll-free (0700), IVR, PBX, audio conferencing. Their NCC license is "Value Added Services SNS" (special numbering services). No USSD capability at all.

## Africa's Talking SMS: YES — this is the simpler option

Instead of USSD-PUSH (which needs a specialized provider like InfoTek), you can just use **AT SMS** to send letters/text to the phone during or after a call. From the session transcripts, this was actually the original Voice + SMS dual-channel design for Phase 2 literacy:

> "Voice teaches the sound, SMS delivers the letter shape. SMS inbox becomes a permanent growing textbook."

### AT SMS Nigeria Pricing

| Provider | Cost per SMS | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **Africa's Talking** | ~₦4-6 per SMS (~$0.003) | [AT Pricing](https://africastalking.com/pricing) — volume-based |
| MTN Bulk SMS | ₦1.95-2.15 per SMS | MTN tiered pricing |
| Bulk SMS providers | ₦2.30-5.62 per SMS | Various Nigerian providers |

### Cost for Phase 2 literacy (SMS to 300 kids)

Phase 2 = 60 literacy calls with letter shapes sent via SMS. Each call might need 2-3 SMS (letter card + example word + practice):

| Scenario | SMS per child | Total SMS | Cost at ₦5/SMS | USD |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Conservative** (2 SMS per call) | 120 | 36,000 | ₦180,000 | **$113** |
| **Standard** (3 SMS per call) | 180 | 54,000 | ₦270,000 | **$169** |

**$113-169 for Phase 2 SMS.** Way simpler than USSD-PUSH — no special provider needed, AT already handles it, works on every phone, and the SMS stays in their inbox as a permanent reference.

### Comparison: SMS vs USSD-PUSH

| | AT SMS | InfoTek USSD-PUSH |
|---|---|---|
| Cost for 300 kids | **$113-169** | **Unknown** (no quote yet) |
| Provider | Already using AT | New provider needed |
| Setup | None — AT SMS API ready | Integration + shared/dedicated short code |
| Works on all phones | Yes | Yes (GSM standard) |
| Persists after call | **Yes** — stays in inbox | **No** — disappears when dismissed |
| Real-time during call | No — arrives after | Yes — displays during call |
| Complexity | Simple — one API call | Complex — dual-provider, SS7 signaling |

SMS is worse for real-time (kid can't see the letter while hearing the sound simultaneously) but better for everything else — cheaper, simpler, persistent, and you already have the provider.

### Bottom line

**Add $150 for AT SMS** to the budget if you want Phase 2 literacy materials delivered digitally. Or keep the printed flashcards ($94) and skip SMS entirely for the pilot.

You don't need Alpha or InfoTek for text delivery. AT does it.

- [AT — Bulk SMS](https://africastalking.com/sms/bulksms)

### What's written (Phase 1 — oral only):

### What's NOT written (Phase 2 — oral + print):

## SMS needed for Phase 2 literacy

Looking at the curriculum design:

**Module 6: Phonics (Weeks 13-16, 16 calls)**

Jolly Phonics order — 7 letter groups:

| Week | Letters | Words built | SMS needed per call |
|---|---|---|---|
| Week 13 (4 calls) | s, a, t, i, p, n | sat, pin, tap, nap, tip, sit | 2 SMS: one with letters (S A T I P N), one with words (SAT, PIN, TAP) |
| Week 14 (4 calls) | c/k, e, h, r, m, d | cat, hen, mat, red, dim | 2 SMS |
| Week 15 (4 calls) | g, o, u, l, f, b | dog, fun, log, but, fig | 2 SMS |
| Week 16 (4 calls) | Review + tricky words | the, is, I, to, a, was + sentences | 3 SMS: letters + tricky words + sentence ("The cat sat") |

**Module 6 subtotal: 16 calls x ~2.25 SMS avg = 36 SMS per child**

**Module 7: Blending & Decodable Reading (Weeks 17-20, 16 calls)**

| Week | Focus | SMS needed |
|---|---|---|
| Week 17 (4 calls) | CVC words (3-letter) | 2 SMS: word list + short sentence |
| Week 18 (4 calls) | CCVC/CVCC (blends — stop, lamp) | 2 SMS: blend words + sentences |
| Week 19 (4 calls) | Digraphs (sh, ch, th, ng) | 2 SMS: digraph pairs + words |
| Week 20 (4 calls) | Simple sentences (5-7 words) | 3 SMS: sentence + questions + new words |

**Module 7 subtotal: 16 calls x ~2.25 SMS avg = 36 SMS per child**

**Module 8: Reading Comprehension With Print (Weeks 21-24, 16 calls)**

| Week | Focus | SMS needed |
|---|---|---|
| Week 21 (4 calls) | Short passage (3-4 sentences) | 3 SMS: passage text (160 chars per SMS, 3-4 sentences needs 2-3 SMS) + questions |
| Week 22 (4 calls) | Informational text | 3 SMS |
| Week 23 (4 calls) | Story with dialogue | 3 SMS |
| Week 24 (4 calls) | Longer passage (6-8 sentences) | 4 SMS: passage spans 3 SMS + questions |

**Module 8 subtotal: 16 calls x ~3.25 SMS avg = 52 SMS per child**

---

## Total SMS per child

| Module | Calls | SMS/call | Total SMS |
|---|---|---|---|
| Module 6 (Phonics) | 16 | 2.25 | 36 |
| Module 7 (Blending) | 16 | 2.25 | 36 |
| Module 8 (Comprehension) | 16 | 3.25 | 52 |
| **Total Phase 2** | **48 calls** | **2.58 avg** | **124 SMS per child** |

## Cost for 300 children

| | SMS count | At ₦5/SMS | USD |
|---|---|---|---|
| Per child | 124 | ₦620 | $0.39 |
| **300 children** | **37,200** | **₦186,000** | **$116** |

So **$116 for all Phase 2 SMS for 300 kids.** Round to **$120**.

But — Phase 2 starts at Month 4 of the course (after 3 months of oral Phase 1). So you don't pay this upfront. It kicks in halfway through the pilot.

**And the scripts still need to be written.** The 48 Phase 2 lesson scripts + 32 remaining numeracy scripts (Division + Word Problems) = **80 scripts to write** before Phase 2 begins. That's the real blocker, not the SMS cost.

## Claude · 2026-04-16T02:21:35.262Z

No. Free tier is fine for 300 kids.

Supabase free tier gives you:
- 500MB database
- 1GB file storage
- 50,000 monthly active users
- Unlimited API requests

300 student profiles with session history, RAG embeddings (916 already seeded), and TaRL assessment data won't come close to 500MB. You'd need thousands of students before hitting that limit.

The only risk is **uptime** — free tier projects pause after 1 week of inactivity. But during an active pilot with daily calls, the database is never inactive.

Cut it. Save $150.

## Claude · 2026-04-16T02:25:45.997Z

From the Foundational Courses Plan:

**Literacy alone is 6 months:**
- Phase 1 (oral): Months 1-3, ~80 calls
- Phase 2 (print): Months 4-6, ~60 calls
- Total: ~140 calls

**Numeracy alone is also 6 months:**
- Modules 1-6: Weeks 1-24, ~100 calls

**But they're designed to run in PARALLEL — interleaved, not sequential.**

From the March 31 session discussion: "TaRL typically does 60-150 hours alternating literacy and numeracy daily." And you settled on **2 calls/day, 5 days/week** — one literacy call and one numeracy call per day.

So the schedule is:

| Time | Morning call | Afternoon call | Total/day |
|---|---|---|---|
| Months 1-3 | Literacy Phase 1 (80 calls) | Numeracy Modules 1-4 (64 calls) | 2 calls |
| Months 4-6 | Literacy Phase 2 (60 calls) | Numeracy Modules 5-6 (36 calls) | 2 calls |
| **Total** | **140 literacy** | **100 numeracy** | **240 calls** |

At 2 calls/day, 5 days/week = 10 calls/week. 240 calls / 10 per week = **24 weeks = 6 months.** Confirmed.

**Total instruction time:** 240 calls x 7 min = 1,680 min = **28 hours.**

From the Literacy Hours Research in folder 3:
- TaRL achieves results in 60-150 hours
- ConnectEd got 0.33 SD in just 3 hours
- World Bank Edo got 1.5-2 years in 13 hours
- Sabi's 28 hours sits between ConnectEd and TaRL — reasonable for AI 1-on-1

**6 months is correct.** The budget is right.

## Cost to Hire the Coordinator

Your situation is different from a typical US hire. You're not posting on job boards or using a recruiter — you're asking Dr. Sonia to recommend someone from her network. So most standard hiring costs don't apply.

| Hiring expense | US typical | Your actual cost | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Job board posting | $200-500 | **$0** | Hiring through personal network (Dr. Sonia, Rhoda, Remi) |
| Recruiter commission | 15-30% of salary | **$0** | No recruiter |
| Background check | $30-100 | **$0** | Dr. Sonia's recommendation IS the background check |
| Interview costs | Travel, time | **$0** | WhatsApp video call from Wesleyan, or in-person during your Lagos trip |
| Onboarding / training | $1,000+ in US | **$50-100** | Print training materials, 2-3 days of shadowing you during Lagos trip. Maybe buy them airtime for the training period. |
| Contractor agreement | $100-500 (lawyer) | **$0-50** | Simple written agreement. Barrister Adejoke can draft this for free as board member. Or use a template. |
| Equipment | Laptop, phone | **$0** | They use their own phone. No laptop needed — they're visiting communities, not doing desk work. |
| **Total hiring cost** | | **$50-100** | |

Call it **$75**.

---

## Camera — Buy Once, Don't Replace

Here's the tier list for "buy it used, keep it for years":

### Best Value: Sony ZV-E10 (used)

| | Details |
|---|---|
| **Used price** | **$300-380** (body + 16-50mm kit lens) |
| Where | [MPB](https://www.mpb.com/en-us/product/sony-zv-e10), [Adorama used](https://www.adorama.com/used-sony-zv-e10-mirrorless-camera-body-black/p/imcsozve10b), eBay, Swappa |
| Warranty | 6 months (MPB), 180 days (Adorama) |
| Sensor | APS-C, 24.3MP |
| Video | 4K 30fps, 1080p 120fps slow-mo |
| Why this one | Interchangeable lenses — you buy the body once, add lenses as budget allows. Flip-out screen for selfie/vlog. Excellent autofocus. Mic input for interviews. The ZV-1 is cheaper but fixed lens = you're stuck. The ZV-E10 grows with you. |
| Lifespan | 5-10 years easy |

### Budget Alternative: Canon EOS R50 (refurbished)

| | Details |
|---|---|
| **Refurbished price** | **$449-499** (body + 18-45mm lens, from Canon Store) |
| Warranty | 1-year Canon USA warranty |
| Video | 4K 30fps (6K oversampled), great autofocus |
| Why | Canon colors look warmer (better for "human" content). But $100-150 more than a used ZV-E10. |

### Cheapest "Real Camera": Sony ZV-1 (used)

| | Details |
|---|---|
| **Used price** | **$200-280** |
| Where | MPB, eBay, Swappa |
| Why | Compact, no extra lenses needed, great video. But fixed lens = can't upgrade. Good enough forever for social media, not ideal if you ever need a wider or longer shot. |

### What I'd buy in your position

**Sony ZV-E10 used with kit lens: ~$350**

- It's the camera you won't have to replace
- Interchangeable lenses mean you can add a $100 prime lens later for interview close-ups
- 4K video for grant applications and pitch decks
- Flip screen for recording yourself
- Mic jack for better audio during interviews
- Small enough to throw in a bag for Lagos

If budget is tight: **Sony ZV-1 used at $230** gets the job done and you never think about lenses.

## Claude · 2026-04-16T04:09:41.432Z

## Teaching at the Right Level (TaRL)

**What it is:** Instead of teaching children by age or grade, you test what they actually know and group them by ability. A 10-year-old reading at a 6-year-old's level gets 6-year-old content — not 10-year-old content they can't understand.

**Who created it:** Pratham (India), early 2000s. Now implemented in 20+ countries through TaRL Africa (formerly Zizi Afrique, rebranded Mizizi Elimu Afrika in March 2026).

**How it works:**
1. Assess every child using ASER tool (5-minute oral test — can you read letters? Words? Paragraphs? A story?)
2. Group by level, not age/grade
3. Teach at THAT level with intensive, focused activities
4. Reassess regularly, move kids up as they improve
5. Typically runs as 30-50 day "learning camps" at 2-3 hours/day

**The evidence (6 RCTs, J-PAL backed):**

| Country | Effect size | What happened |
|---|---|---|
| India (multiple states) | 0.10-0.71 SD | 19% readers → 79% among 346,000 children |
| Madagascar | 0.56 SD | ~2 years of learning gains |
| Nigeria (7 states) | 12-38 pp gains | Active through Human Capital Africa |
| Uganda (Building Tomorrow) | 78% moved up 1+ level | 25 days, ~40 hours |

**Scale:** 80 million+ children reached globally.

**Classification:** GEEAP (Global Education Evidence Advisory Panel) rates it a **"Great Buy"** — the most cost-effective category. Less than $10/child.

**Why it matters for Sabi:** TaRL is exactly what Sabi does — but with AI instead of human facilitators. The diagnostic placement, the level-based teaching, the reassessment. The difference is a human facilitator handles 30 kids in a room. Sabi handles one child at a time on a phone — true 1-on-1 at the right level.

**Key sources:**
- [J-PAL — TaRL Evidence](https://www.povertyactionlab.org/case-study/teaching-right-level-improve-learning)
- [TaRL Africa](https://teachingattherightlevel.org/)
- [Pratham](https://www.pratham.org/about/teaching-at-the-right-level/)

## Naomi · 2026-04-16T04:12:43.561Z

what did they do though? it's on my slide for "this approach is proven"

## Claude · 2026-04-16T04:12:56.129Z

They grouped children by what they could actually do — not by age or grade — and gave them intensive, focused practice at that level using trained community volunteers and teachers.

Specifically:

- **Assessed every child** with a simple oral test (can you recognize letters? Read words? Read a paragraph?)
- **Grouped them by ability** — a 10-year-old who can't read gets grouped with 7-year-olds who also can't read, not with 10-year-olds doing grade-level work
- **30-50 days of focused instruction**, 2-3 hours/day
- **Volunteers and teachers trained** in TaRL methodology — simple, structured activities (not lecturing)
- **Reassessed regularly** and moved kids up when ready
- **School management committees** were also strengthened so the school system supported it

The key insight: they didn't add more school. They didn't buy tablets. They didn't hire more teachers. They just **stopped pretending every child was at grade level** and taught them where they actually were. That alone — meeting kids where they are — produced 2 years of learning gains.

For your slide, the one-liner: **"Grouped children by ability, not age. Taught at their level. 2 years of gains in weeks. $10/child."**

## Naomi · 2026-04-16T04:23:52.225Z

## Claude · 2026-04-16T04:24:04.086Z

In 2024, the World Bank ran a randomized controlled trial in Edo State, Nigeria. They put about 800 senior secondary students in after-school computer labs, sat them in front of desktop computers, and let them chat with GPT-4 through Microsoft Copilot. Twelve sessions, 90 minutes each, over six weeks. A teacher supervised but the AI did the teaching.

The results shocked everyone. Students gained the equivalent of 1.5 to 2 years of learning in six weeks. The benefit-cost ratio — 161 to 260 — was the highest the World Bank had ever measured for any education intervention, anywhere. At $48 per student.

But here's what matters for Sabi: those students were 15-17 years old, could already read and write, used desktop computers with internet, and had a teacher in the room. That's the best-case scenario — literate teenagers with screens and supervision.

Sabi reaches the kids that study can't touch. Eight-year-olds who can't read a single word, on a $5 phone with no internet, no teacher, no screen. If AI tutoring produces 2 years of gains under ideal conditions, the question is: how much can it produce under real ones? That's what our pilot answers.

## Claude · 2026-04-16T06:47:35.070Z

From the load test (March 31): **1 GPU handles 300-500 students.** After that, TTS chokes because Whisper + Chatterbox + Ollama fight over 20GB VRAM.

| Students | GPUs needed | Monthly cost | 6-month cost | Per student |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 300 | 1 | $203 | **$1,218** | **$4.06** |
| 500 | 1 | $203 | **$1,218** | **$2.44** |
| 1,000 | 2-3 | $406-609 | **$2,436-3,654** | **$2.44-3.65** |
| 5,000 | 10-15 | $2,030-3,045 | **$12,180-18,270** | **$2.44-3.65** |
| 10,000 | 20-30 | $4,060-6,090 | **$24,360-36,540** | **$2.44-3.65** |
| 100,000 | 200-300 | $40,600-60,900 | **$243,600-365,400** | **$2.44-3.65** |

It's basically **linear** — cost per student stays flat at $2.44-3.65 because each GPU serves the same number of kids. No economies of scale on the server side.

**BUT** — with split architecture (separate voice GPUs + separate LLM GPUs), each server does more because there's no VRAM contention:

| Students | Voice servers | LLM servers | Total monthly | 6-month cost | Per student |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 300 | 1 | 0 (use Claude API) | $203 | **$1,218** | **$4.06** |
| 1,000 | 1 | 1 | $406 | **$2,436** | **$2.44** |
| 5,000 | 1 | 2 | $609 | **$3,654** | **$0.73** |
| 10,000 | 2 | 3 | $1,015 | **$6,090** | **$0.61** |
| 100,000 | 15 | 20 | $7,105 | **$42,630** | **$0.43** |

Split architecture **does** scale — voice servers handle ~2,000 students each (no VRAM competition), LLM servers handle even more (text processing is fast).

**The move from all-in-one to split architecture is the key cost unlock.** Same Hetzner hardware, just dedicated roles. Goes from $3.65/student to $0.43/student at 100K.

For the pilot at 300 kids: doesn't matter, 1 server either way. This only matters at 1,000+.

## Naomi · 2026-04-16T06:49:49.806Z

why do we need more LLM servers and less voice serbbers?

## Claude · 2026-04-16T06:50:10.700Z

Because the LLM is the bottleneck, not voice.

**Voice (Whisper STT + Chatterbox TTS):** Each request is a quick burst — Whisper transcribes 7 seconds of audio in ~0.5s, Chatterbox generates a response in ~1.5s. Then the GPU sits idle for 30-60 seconds while the child listens and speaks. The GPU is busy maybe 5% of the call. One voice server can juggle hundreds of calls because they're mostly waiting.

**LLM (Ollama Llama 3.1 8B):** Generating a response takes ~2-4 seconds of continuous GPU compute. And unlike voice where you wait for the child, LLM requests stack up — if 20 kids finish speaking at the same moment, that's 20 LLM requests queued. The GPU is busy much more of the time.

So at scale:

| Component | GPU time per turn | Idle time between turns | Concurrent capacity |
|---|---|---|---|
| Voice (STT + TTS) | ~2 seconds | ~40 seconds (child listening/talking) | **High** — 1 server handles ~2,000 kids |
| LLM | ~3 seconds | ~40 seconds | **Lower** — requests cluster and queue |

You need more LLM servers because when 5,000 kids are calling, the LLM requests bunch together (everyone finishes listening at roughly the same intervals) and create spikes. Voice requests are spread out naturally because STT and TTS happen at different moments in each call.

That said — at pilot (300 kids), this is irrelevant. One server does everything. This only matters when you're past 1,000.

- $42,630 / 100,000 = **$0.43**

At 500,000 I just did:
- 250 voice + 350 LLM = 600 servers
- $0.43 x 5 should still be **$0.43/student**

The problem is I used different ratios. At 100K I assumed 1 voice server per ~6,667 students and 1 LLM per ~5,000. At 500K I assumed 1 voice per ~2,000 and 1 LLM per ~1,429. Way more conservative.

The 100K number was optimistic. The 500K number was pessimistic. The honest answer depends on which server capacity estimate you trust. From the load test, **300-500 students per GPU all-in-one.** Split architecture roughly doubles that.

## Claude · 2026-04-16T06:53:38.337Z

Instead of running Whisper + Chatterbox + Ollama on the same GPU (they fight over 20GB VRAM and everything slows down), you dedicate servers to one job:

**Voice servers:** Only run Whisper STT + Chatterbox TTS. Uses ~8.5GB VRAM. No LLM competing. Fast.

**LLM servers:** Only run Ollama Llama 3.1 8B. Uses ~6-8GB VRAM. No voice models competing. Fast.

When a child speaks:
1. Audio goes to a **voice server** → Whisper transcribes → text
2. Text goes to an **LLM server** → Ollama generates response → text
3. Text goes back to a **voice server** → Chatterbox speaks → audio back to child

Same hardware ($203/mo each). Same Hetzner GEX44. Just dedicated roles instead of cramming everything on one machine. Each server handles more students because there's no VRAM contention.

That's what the load test proved — the bottleneck isn't any single model, it's all three fighting for the same GPU at the same time.

For the pilot (300 kids): doesn't matter, one server does everything. Split architecture is a scale optimization for 1,000+.

The **all-in-one** is ~$2.44-3.65/student because each GPU only handles 300-500 kids (VRAM contention).

The **split** drops it to ~$1.48/student because each dedicated server handles more kids (~2,000 for voice, ~1,400 for LLM).

| Architecture | Per student (6 months) | When |
|---|---|---|
| **All-in-one** | **$2.44-3.65** | 300-1,000 kids |
| **Split** | **~$1.48** | 1,000+ kids |

The savings from split is **40-60% cheaper** than all-in-one. But after that, it's linear because there's no shared overhead that gets amortized — each server is doing the same job at the same capacity.

The only way to push per-student cost lower from here:

| Optimization | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Bigger GPU (Hetzner GEX131, 96GB VRAM)** | Fits all 3 models with zero contention on one machine. Handles ~5,000+ kids. $920/mo instead of 3x $203 = $609. But per-student still roughly the same. |
| **Faster/smaller models** | Whisper medium instead of large-v3, Phi-3.5 Mini instead of Llama 8B — less VRAM, faster inference, more concurrent calls per server |
| **Cerebras API for LLM** | $0.0012/call instead of a whole GPU. Eliminates LLM servers entirely. Voice-only servers + Cerebras = much cheaper at scale |

Bottom line: split gets you from $3.65 to $1.48. After that it's flat unless you change the models or architecture.

## Cerebras — The Short Version

They built a custom chip (the size of a dinner plate — literally the world's largest chip) specifically for AI inference. Result: **insanely fast, insanely cheap.**

### Speed

| Provider | Llama 3.1 8B speed | Sabi LLM response time |
|---|---|---|
| **Cerebras** | **1,800-2,000 tokens/sec** | **<0.1 seconds** |
| Ollama on your Hetzner GPU | ~120 tokens/sec | ~1.7 seconds |
| Claude Haiku API | ~150 tokens/sec | ~1.5 seconds |

Cerebras is **15x faster** than your self-hosted Ollama. The LLM response becomes essentially instant.

### Cost

**$0.10 per million tokens.** For Sabi:

- Per call: ~11,900 tokens (1,550 input + 150 output per turn x 7 turns)
- Cost per call: **$0.0012**
- Per student (240 calls): **$0.29**

Compare:

| LLM option | Per student (240 calls) | Monthly (300 kids) |
|---|---|---|
| **Cerebras Llama 3.1 8B** | **$0.29** | **$14** |
| Claude Haiku API | $1.08 | $54 |
| Self-hosted Ollama (GPU cost) | $1.48 (split architecture) | $74 (server share) |

**Cerebras is 5x cheaper than your own GPU for the LLM alone.**

### What this means for Sabi at scale

If you use Cerebras for LLM, your GPU servers only run voice (Whisper + Chatterbox). No LLM servers needed at all.

| Students | Voice servers | LLM | Monthly GPU | Cerebras/mo | Total/mo | 6 months | Per student |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 300 | 1 | Cerebras | $203 | $14 | **$217** | **$1,302** | **$4.34** |
| 1,000 | 1 | Cerebras | $203 | $48 | **$251** | **$1,506** | **$1.51** |
| 5,000 | 3 | Cerebras | $609 | $242 | **$851** | **$5,106** | **$1.02** |
| 30,000 | 15 | Cerebras | $3,045 | $1,450 | **$4,495** | **$26,970** | **$0.90** |
| 100,000 | 50 | Cerebras | $10,150 | $4,833 | **$14,983** | **$89,898** | **$0.90** |
| 300,000 | 150 | Cerebras | $30,450 | $14,500 | **$44,950** | **$269,700** | **$0.90** |
| 1,000,000 | 500 | Cerebras | $101,500 | $48,333 | **$149,833** | **$898,998** | **$0.90** |

**$0.90/student at scale.** Down from $1.48 with self-hosted LLM.

And unlike self-hosted Ollama, Cerebras **does scale better** — because the Cerebras cost per call is fixed ($0.0012) while you need fewer GPU servers (voice-only handles more concurrent calls than all-in-one).

### The tradeoff

| | Self-hosted Ollama | Cerebras API |
|---|---|---|
| Cost at 300 kids | $4.06/student (all-in-one) | $4.34/student |
| Cost at 100K+ kids | $1.48/student | **$0.90/student** |
| Speed | 1.7s per response | **<0.1s per response** |
| Dependency | None — you own the hardware | Cerebras stays online and keeps pricing |
| Data privacy | Everything on your server | Student conversations go through Cerebras API |
| Offline capability | Works if internet dies | Doesn't work without internet |

### Bottom line

For the pilot (300 kids): doesn't matter, use your existing GPU with Ollama. 

For scale (5,000+): **Cerebras eliminates LLM servers entirely, cuts cost to $0.90/student, and makes responses instant.** The risk is API dependency — but you keep Ollama on your voice servers as a fallback.
